schools.summary: Augustine calls it a short psalm, satisfying the mental cravings of its hearers without taxing those who are fasting, and takes the cast-down soul to be cast down from hunger — for fasting is voluntary and being an-hungered is not. What is an-hungered is the Church, that Man extended through the whole world whose Head is above and limbs below; and on the plea itself he is unafraid, not dreading the judgment because he knows the mercy, though in this pilgrimage he must live with the tares until the harvest.

Calvin reports that most critics take this and the preceding psalm as originally one, forty-six manuscripts still printing them so, and passes on Williams's account of choristers who divided an over-long anthem for their own convenience; he has David driven from his country by the violence of his enemies, calling on God for vengeance and encouraging himself to hope for restoration. Gill notes the Targum's addition, with the judgment of truth.

Henry reads the opening plea as two lawsuits at once — defendant against those who impeached him, appealing from their courts to the court of heaven, and plaintiff against those who injured him — and observes that the unmerciful show themselves ungodly, since anyone with fear or love of the master has compassion on his fellow-servants; Spurgeon takes the appeal as a willingness to be examined, content that God should weigh his character, since one good word from God outweighs ten thousand railing speeches of men.

Clarke counts the manuscripts that join the psalm to the one before, notes that Hebrew and Chaldee give it no title, reports the Syriac and Arabic headings, and names the enemies outright as the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar; he calls the opening phrase forensic, rightly rendered plead my cause. Wesley takes the nation for the sheer number of David's adversaries and guesses the man to be Ahithophel or Absalom.
Ellicott works on the word for ungodly, which in Hebrew is simply a negative term — a nation not in the covenant — though a positive idea of wickedness would naturally come to attach to it.

debates.question: Who are the ungodly nation and the unjust man?

sides.position: the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar, the psalm continuing the captives’ complaint
David's own enemies — Saul, or Ahithophel or Absalom

debates.question: Is this a separate psalm from the forty-second?

sides.position: no — style, sentiment, metre and the refrain make it one, and forty-six manuscripts print it so

2.pericope_label: Send out thy light: the altar and the returning refrain

schools.summary: Gill takes the God of my strength for the giver of strength natural and spiritual, and the strength of heart, life and salvation; he opens the light three ways — the Messiah, the Spirit, the Gospel — before preferring the light of God's countenance, and the truth as Christ, or the word of truth, or God's faithfulness; the altar he sets in the tabernacle, adding that under the Gospel it is Christ.

Spurgeon presses past the furniture to what it is for: it is not his own house David's willing feet would seek first but the altar, though it was not the altar as such he cared for, being no believer in ritualism — what are the rites of worship unless the Lord be in them but empty shells and dry husks? He marks the rapture of the title, God being not his joy only but his exceeding joy, not the fountain or giver of joy but that joy itself.

Clarke keeps the captives speaking throughout — why are we cast off, now that we are humbled and penitent? — reads light and truth as answering the two halves of the trouble, and turns the closing refrain into an argument for patience, since the word concerning the captivity was for an appointed time and will not finally tarry. Wesley glosses the sending as an actual discovery of them, and the hill as Zion, the place of God's presence and worship.

Ellicott draws the contrast that gives the petition its force — instead of the guard who led the exile away from the holy hill, light and truth are asked for as two angel guides to lead him back, the Urim and Thummim of the saints — and notes that God my God is this collection's form for the more usual Jehovah my God; Keil and Delitzsch describe the movement as anticipation, the poet revelling beforehand in what he prayed for, knowing no higher aim than to be again where the fountainhead of that joy is.

debates.question: What are the light and the truth that are to lead?

sides.position: two angel guides, the Urim and Thummim of the saints, escorting the exile home
a favourable turn of affairs and the fulfilment of the promises
perhaps the Messiah, the Spirit or the Gospel, but likeliest the light of God’s countenance and his faithfulness

themes: send out thy light and thy truth
thy holy hill and thy tabernacles
